name: Internal quality factor of niobium quarter-wave CPW resonators (4-8 GHz) versus drive power down to the single-photon level at 10 mK
plain_name: Measure how much microwave energy a superconducting resonator chip loses, down to single photons
description: Wire-bond a 5 x 7 mm chip of niobium coplanar-waveguide quarter-wavelength resonators (4-8 GHz) into a sample box, cool it to 10 mK in a cryogen-free dilution refrigerator and sweep the VNA drive power over about 90 dB (roughly 1e-2 to 1e7 photons) through 60 dB of cold attenuation and a 4 K HEMT to extract internal and loaded Q, as in the Chalmers resonator-optimisation thesis.
keywords: Measure how much microwave energy a superconducting resonator chip loses, down to single photons

sources.citation: Characterisation and optimisation of superconducting microwave resonators (T. Boehme, MSc thesis, Chalmers University of Technology, 2016)

reported_equipment: high electron mobility transistor (HEMT) amplifier of about 35 dB at the 4 K stage

requirements.rationale: The resonators were measured at 10 mK, far below Tc, to suppress thermal quasiparticles and thermal photons; the fridge base must reach 10 mK.
Resonance frequencies span 4-8 GHz, so the cold coaxial input/output chain must transmit up to 8 GHz.
The chip is 5 mm x 7 mm; its circumscribed diameter is sqrt(5^2+7^2) = 8.602 mm, rounded up to 8603 um, which the sample space must accept.
The chip is wire bonded to a PCB in a sample box with K connectors; RF connections to the sample are required.
Optional: the source used a pulse-tube-precooled (cryogen-free) dilution refrigerator; a wet fridge reaching 10 mK would also work.

confirmation_note: Requirements taken from the cited procedure and independently re-verified against the source (research/v4, 2026-11-01). Users must confirm them for their own run; edits require confirmation again.
